⚠️ Illustrative modeling tool — not tax advice
This is an educational model for illustrative purposes only. It simplifies a complex area of tax law, and errors are possible. The outputs are estimates, not a tax return, an opinion, or a recommendation. Do not act on these numbers — verify every figure with your own qualified tax advisor. The model assumes the deal's make-or-break position holds: that your losses are non-passive because you materially participate under §469 (the >100-hour Test 3 in Treas. Reg. §1.469-5T(a)(3)). If that fails, the Year-1 deduction cannot offset your wages as shown. FEDERAL INCOME TAX ONLY — NO STATE TAX (many states do not conform to federal bonus depreciation; model your state separately)

Heavy Machinery — Tax Modeling Application

A federal income-tax model for buying heavy equipment into the Highland Steel / EZ Equipment Zone “Advantage Flex” rental program through your LLC. It shows the Year-1 depreciation shelter, the annual lease income and deductible interest, and the §1245 recapture at the Year-6 buyback. Change any input and every number, table, and chart recomputes live.

FEDERAL · 2026 BRACKETS (Rev. Proc. 2025-32) · SINGLE or MFJ · NOT TAX ADVICE

This tool answers one question: what does buying heavy equipment into this program do to your federal taxes — in Year 1, every year you hold it, and in the year you exit? It is built to be read by someone seeing it for the first time, so every field, table, and chart is labeled and explained. Tip: click any blue i for help, click any headline result box for a full breakdown with charts, and click any underlined number in the detail table to see how it was computed.

STEP 1 · Set your tax picture
Pick Single or MFJ, enter your income for each year, and set your personal deductions. Lower a later year to model exiting in a low-income (retirement) year.
STEP 2 · Set the deal
Equipment value, down payment, loan rate/term, depreciation method, exit year, and the buyback %. Lease income auto-fills to the program figure.
STEP 3 · Read the tax effect
The Tax Modeling tab shows the year-by-year picture; the Tax Waterfall tab shows which brackets your savings and recapture land in.
How the tax math works (read this once) ▾

Year 1 — the deduction. The equipment is mobile §1245 business property, so under §168(k) (or §179) you may deduct 100% of its purchase price the first year — not just your 10% cash down, because your personal guarantee of the loan puts the full price “at risk” under §465. That deduction comes off the top of your income, saving tax at your highest marginal rates first. The lease income, deductible interest, and platform fee are folded in; the net is a large Year-1 business loss.

The make-or-break gate (§469). That loss only offsets your W-2/active income if you materially participate — the deal relies on Test 3 (>100 hours and not less than anyone else). If you don’t clear it, the losses become passive and can’t offset wages. The opinion letter rates this “more likely than not.” This model assumes it holds.

The §461(l) limit. A W-2 earner can only use a business loss up to $512,000 MFJ / $256,000 single against other income in one year (2026). Any excess isn’t lost — it becomes a Net Operating Loss (NOL) carried forward, usable at up to 80% of income per year under §172. The tool tracks this automatically.

Every year you hold it — the income. The equipment earns lease income (net of the program’s insurance, maintenance, and subscription fees). After the deductible interest, that’s taxable income that adds a little tax back each year.

The year you exit — the recapture. Depreciation is a deferral, not a gift. At the Year-6 buyback (a 56% floor), §1245 recaptures the depreciation as ordinary income, stacked on that year’s income. Under 100% bonus your basis is zero, so the entire buyback is recaptured. If you’re still high-income that year, it stacks into your top brackets — which is why exit-year income is the single biggest lever you control.

Kept simple on purpose. This is federal income tax only. It does not model state income tax (many states do not conform to federal bonus depreciation — which can substantially reduce the state-level benefit), self-employment tax, NIIT, AMT, or QBI, and it doesn’t model reinvesting the tax savings (the program’s time-value case). Use it to understand the shape of the tax effect, then confirm the dollars with your CPA.

The whole story in six numbers. Green = money in your pocket; red = tax you owe. Click a box for a step-by-step breakdown.

Bonus vs MACRS — side by side — same inputs, both methods

Bonus front-loads the entire write-off (biggest Year-1 shelter, full recapture at exit); MACRS spreads it and leaves basis behind, usually a smaller recapture. The toggle above sets which one drives the rest of the tool; this card always shows both.

Year-by-Year Federal Tax

Grey bars are the tax you’d pay with no deal; blue bars are your tax with the equipment (in the exit year the blue bar includes the recapture, so it spikes). The dark navy line is the net tax effect each year (saving = +, cost = −). The amber dashed line is the cumulative net effect — the running total across all years — so you can see, at any year, whether the deal is still ahead or has been overtaken by the recapture.

Cash flow over the hold — waterfall

Every cash movement, in order: your cash down (out), then each year’s tax saving plus operating cash (the exit year also folds in the net sale), and the final all-in bar. Green bars add cash, red bars take it away; the navy bar is where you end up.

The time-value case — reinvesting the Year-1 savings

The program’s core argument: bank the big Year-1 tax saving and invest it. The grey line holds it as cash; the green line reinvests it at your assumed rate. If the green line clears the red recapture line by exit, the reinvested savings alone cover the tax you owe at the buyback — the “kick the can, then pay it from growth” case.

Assumed annual return on the banked savings. Decimal: 0.05 = 5%.

Tax Waterfall — Where Your Dollars Land in the Brackets

Two “bracket walks”: how your Year-1 deduction saves tax (walking down from the top of your income), and how the exit-year recapture costs tax (stacking up on top of your income). Both on taxable income, so the savings shown are real.

① Year-1 Bracket Walk — your deduction, and the real tax it saves

The top bar is your Year-1 taxable income with no deal; the bottom bar is with the equipment. The brackets that vanish are your deduction — and because they are the top (highest-rate) brackets, that is where the big saving comes from.

② Exit-Year Bracket Walk — the recapture, and what it costs

The top bar is your exit-year taxable income without the recapture; the bottom bar adds the recapture on top — pushing you into darker, higher-rate brackets. Lower your exit-year income (a retirement year) and the recapture falls into cheaper brackets.

The arbitrage — deduct high, recapture low?

A deferral only “wins” on taxes if the rate you deduct at exceeds the rate you recapture at. The biggest lever you control is the exit-year income: exiting in a low-income year pushes the recapture into cheaper brackets and flips the spread in your favor.

The Loan & The Exit

The loan fully amortizes over its term. Two things to understand: how the balance pays down, and what the Year-6 buyback nets you after the recapture and the remaining loan payoff.

Loan balance over time

The financed balance amortizes down over the term. At your exit year the remaining balance is paid off out of the buyback proceeds — the shorter your hold vs. the amortization term, the more balance is left to settle.

Loan Amortization Schedule

Each year: opening balance, the payment, and how it splits between deductible interest and non-deductible principal. Interest is high early and falls as the balance drops.

Net cash at exit, by buyback value

For your exit year, what you net from the buyback at each possible value: proceeds, minus the loan balance you still owe, minus the recapture tax. A higher buyback brings more recapture — the recapture eats much of any premium. The table shows the math behind each bar.

Glossary — every term used in this tool

Bonus depreciation (§168(k))
A deduction equal to 100% of the equipment’s cost, taken in the year it’s placed in service. OBBBA made 100% permanent for property placed in service after 1/19/2025. The deal also qualifies for §179 expensing.
MACRS
The alternative to bonus: the cost is recovered over a fixed schedule (here the 5-year, 200% declining-balance, half-year table typical for construction equipment) instead of all in Year 1. Leaves basis behind, so a smaller recapture at exit.
Material participation (§469)
For the losses to offset your wages (non-passive), you must materially participate. The deal relies on Test 3 — more than 100 hours and not less than any other individual. The opinion letter rates this “more likely than not.”
At-risk basis (§465)
You can only deduct losses up to the amount you have “at risk.” Your personal guarantee of the recourse loan puts the full equipment cost at risk — the basis for deducting the whole price, not just your cash down.
§1245 recapture
On the sale/buyback of depreciated equipment, the depreciation you took is taxed back as ordinary income, stacked on that year’s income. Unavoidable on a taxable sale.
Adjusted basis (§1011/§1016)
Cost minus depreciation taken. Gain = buyback − adjusted basis; it drives the recapture. Under 100% bonus the basis is $0, so the whole buyback is recaptured.
Excess Business Loss cap (§461(l))
The most a business loss can offset against your other income in one year — $512,000 MFJ / $256,000 single (2026). The excess becomes an NOL.
NOL carryforward (§172)
A loss you couldn’t use this year, carried forward — limited to offsetting 80% of a year’s taxable income. This tool tracks and draws it down automatically.
Lease income
The rental income the equipment earns through the program, net of insurance, maintenance, and the platform subscription fee. The program targets ~$11,050/month per $1M of equipment but does not guarantee it.
Amortizing loan & balloon
The loan amortizes over ~10 years but the program term is 6 years, so a balance remains at exit — paid off out of the buyback proceeds.
Buyback (56% floor)
At 72 months, the operating partner repurchases the equipment at a contractual floor of 56% of the original price. This is your exit value and it triggers the recapture.
Bracket walk
A picture of which tax brackets a deduction (walking down from the top of your income) or income (stacking up) falls into.

What this tool deliberately leaves out

Federal income tax only. State income tax is not modeled — many states do not conform to federal bonus depreciation, so residents of a non-conforming state need a separate state schedule (your CPA handles that). Also not modeled: self-employment tax, §1411 NIIT, AMT, and §199A QBI. The material-participation (§469) and at-risk (§465) positions are assumptions the deal takes. If you sell above cost, capital-gains treatment applies to the excess. Reinvestment/compounding of the tax savings is not modeled (the deal's time-value case). Use this to understand the SHAPE of the tax effect, then confirm the dollars with your own CPA.
